item.title: Great Customer Service Comes in All Shapes and Sizes
item.description:
Career

Great Customer Service Comes in All Shapes and Sizes

Effective service often involves "putting yourself in someone else's shoes."

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Exceptional service is about attitude and empathy, not age or experience.
  • Active listening is key to understanding and addressing customers’ needs.
  • Calmness and non-defensive responses can help de-escalate challenging situations.
  • Genuine enjoyment of helping people sets great service providers apart.

As I was paying my bill at a small business recently (we’ll leave the business unnamed to protect the innocent), I was momentarily surprised when I came to the counter. The young employee behind it could barely see over it.

She was probably 14 (the minimum age for summer-job retail work) and couldn’t have been much over 4 feet tall.

Exceptional customer service can be more a function of attitude than age.
Source: Tima Miroschnichenko / Pexels

But any temporary uncertainty I may have had evaporated the moment she opened her mouth and began confidently addressing me.

"You’re here to pay?” she said, “well, let’s get you taken care of.”

She navigated the electronic payment terminal deftly, processed my payment efficiently, and then asked (which her predecessors in the role often forgot to do): “Would you like to make another appointment?”

We agreed on a future date and time. “Thank you for your business,” she said courteously, “we’ll look forward to seeing you again soon.”

I know the proprietor of the business, having frequented it regularly for several years now. She knows I’m interested in management, and at times we’ve chatted about the challenges of small business ownership.

As I was walking out, I happened to see her. “Well,” I said, pausing halfway out the door, “I just received some excellent service from your very capable new employee.”

She chuckled, nodded, and said to me quietly, “If I could clone her, I would.”

Elements of Excellence

This interaction made me think about the elements of excellent service—a function that in one form or another is vital to almost all businesses. What is it that makes some people unusually good at it?

I know there are plenty of ways to skin this cat; you could probably come up with 50 reasonably important service attributes. So, after a career in business, the following are my personal top three.

Listening is foundational. You have to be competent in a role, of course, to know the basics of what’s involved, and then actively listen to assess what a customer needs. Or to understand what they’re upset about, or what their issues might be. The ability to listen carefully and take in information without judgment is a key component of any service role.

Calmness is critical. Providing good service involves being present in the moment and focusing without getting flustered. Being able to converse without being defensive. Having sometimes been in this role myself (as head of advertising, I was frequently working with and providing service to the company’s top sales representatives), I know it’s easier said than done to remain calm when someone is verbally “attacking” you. Often the simple act of listening respectfully when a person is venting and then responding non-defensively can go a long way toward resolving a situation.

Last but definitely not least is empathy. My own impression is that individuals who succeed in a service role genuinely like people, enjoy interacting with them, and want to help solve their problems. Being able to “put yourself in someone else’s shoes” and understand how they might be feeling is an important piece of the service puzzle. How would you like to be treated if you were in their position?

There are more valuable service qualities for sure; this list is personal and by no means exhaustive. These are just three boxes to check. It felt like my young friend who inspired this small story checked all of them.

item.title: Reading Fiction Connects Us to the Human Story
item.description:
Empathy

Reading Fiction Connects Us to the Human Story

When we read stories, we understand and empathize with others.

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Reading for pleasure facilitates the development of prosocial skills.
  • Reading can alleviate loneliness and social isolation.
  • Adults who read more tend to live longer, healthier lives.

It is all over the news and social media—paradoxically, we are lonelier and more disconnected from others than ever before, even as we spend more and more time online. Adolescents and young adults, in particular, are facing a mental health crisis, experiencing anxiety and social isolation at unprecedented rates.

Alongside these headlines are seemingly unrelated stories: Americans are reading for pleasure at lower rates than ever before. Lisa Bonos in The Washington Post reports on multiple research studies in the U.S. and in London over the last few decades that indicate that only 16 percent of the adult population reads for pleasure every day, and 46 percent have read no books at all in the last year.

What does this have to do with loneliness? Intriguingly, not reading fiction and feeling socially isolated may, in fact, be related. It is stories that connect us, to both characters in books and people in real life. When we listen to stories, we understand and empathize with others, key components of feeling connected.

Raymond Mar and his colleagues have been studying the effects of reading fiction for years, and they have just published a review summarizing the many benefits. Not surprisingly, people who read more fiction have better vocabularies and do better academically. But the benefits of reading extend far beyond these cognitive abilities.

Children who read more fiction show higher levels of empathy and demonstrate more prosocial behavior. As Mar argues, reading fiction places us in complex narrative worlds, reading about the exploits and the inner lives of characters—characters that we may like and identify with, or even those we dislike and want to distance ourselves from. Either way, reading helps us understand what makes humans “tick,” why they behave as they do, what their motivations, intentions, and emotions are, and what the consequences of their behaviors are.

As we read, we become embedded in worlds and lives not our own. Yet in this immersion, we come to understand these different worlds, different perspectives, different ways of being. Reading connects us to other minds, even if those minds are fictional.

I have been an avid reader for as long as I can remember. I was a very shy child, a fact that my friends today find hard to believe. I thought of books as my escape, escape from the social anxiety, the sense of not belonging, the sense of being unable to connect. I escaped into worlds that I knew little about culturally or historically—Heidi, Anne of Green Gables, Nancy Drew, and Cherry Ames. Reading allowed me entry into different identities, different viewpoints, different worlds. I could “try on” all kinds of ways of being, explore different identities, be different people in my head. And through this, I developed skills for connecting with people in real life—to learn their stories, their viewpoints, to enter into a world with them and connect.

In their review of the research, Mar and colleagues point to the lifelong benefits of reading fiction—adults who read more fiction are less prejudiced, more insightful, and more reflective about life. They are also more cognitively flexible: reading fiction increases neuronal connectivity. It actually makes our brains healthier! And this increases our physical well-being. People who read more fiction show less cognitive decline with age and actually live longer. Wow, books are powerful!

Reading fiction is not a substitute for real-life social interaction in real life, but it may strengthen our skills for social interaction skills. By helping us understand myriad people facing myriad challenges and by building empathy and perspective-taking, reading fiction may “grease the wheels,” so to speak. This may be one reason why book clubs, both in person and online, are on the rise—talking together about the books we read may help us talk more about life in general, share our own stories, and connect.

But what if you are not a reader? If you have not yet developed this habit, what can you do? In Brain Matters, Richard Sima gives advice. First, start slow—try to read at least 10 minutes a day. And do it consistently to build a habit.

And start reading any book that seems interesting to you—a short story, a graphic novel, sci-fi, romance, whatever grabs your attention. And remember, reading is fun! Just like sharing stories with other people, relax, let yourself go, don’t stress over it. You just may find yourself immersed in a different world, experiencing new perspectives, laughing out loud, or shedding tears. Reading connects us to the human story. And to each other.
